stories.event: Rabbi Yishmael had two scholars judge a case of a sharecropper who had brought him fruits, and found himself mentally arguing the litigant's side.
stories.turn: He realized that even without taking a bribe he was biased.
stories.outcome: He cursed those who take bribes, concluding they are surely far more biased.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael recused himself and seated two scholars to judge the case. As he walked about he kept thinking of arguments for the man who had brought him the fruit. He exclaimed that if he, who took nothing that was not his, was so swayed, how much more so are those who take bribes.

stories.event: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from far away.
stories.turn: Questioned, the man admitted he had a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, recused himself, and found himself biased in the man's favor anyway, cursing bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man came from a distant place to give the priest Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing. When asked why he had not given it to a nearer priest, he said he had a case before him. Rabbi Yishmael declared himself disqualified, refused the gift and had two scholars judge it, yet still caught himself thinking of the man's arguments, and concluded how much more biased real bribe-takers must be.

stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish; Rav Anan refused it as he had a case, but accepted it after the man said he wanted to honor a scholar, and referred the case to Rav Nahman.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative, gave him precedence and honor, and the opposing litigant was intimidated and lost.
stories.outcome: Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan; after fasting and prayer Elijah returned but frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box to learn, producing the two Orders of Elijah.
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan fish; Rav Anan refused because the man had a case, but when the man said he wanted to fulfill the mitzva of giving a gift to a scholar, he accepted it and sent the man with a letter to Rav Nahman, saying he was disqualified. Rav Nahman took him for a relative of Rav Anan, put aside an orphans' case and honored him, so his opponent was cowed and lost. Elijah, who had been teaching Rav Anan, stopped coming; Rav Anan fasted and Elijah returned, but now frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box before him, which is why there is a Major and a Minor Seder Eliyahu.

stories.actor: A wife who brought two maidservants into her marriage
stories.event: Her husband married a second wife and gave one of the first wife's maidservants to the second.
stories.turn: She cried out before Rava about the injustice.
stories.outcome: Rava ignored her complaint.
stories.summary: A woman brought two maidservants into her marriage. Her husband married another woman and assigned one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came crying to Rava, but he paid no attention to her.

stories.actor: A glass-bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give'.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that such a reply means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was selling glass beads, and a woman asked him for a string. He asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it to her, and she said, 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this mocking reply is nothing.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She said 'Give me to drink, give me to drink'.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that this reply is nothing.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup of wine. He asked if she would be betrothed to him with it, and she said, 'Pour, pour me a drink.' Rav Hama ruled she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A man picking dates and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with them.
stories.turn: She said 'Throw, throw'.
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that this reply is nothing.
stories.summary: A man was knocking dates off a palm, and a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked if she would be betrothed to him with them, and she said, 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled she was not betrothed.

stories.event: A woman visiting her husband's grave had relations with a guard of an executed man's body.
stories.turn: The body he guarded was taken.
stories.outcome: She removed her husband's body from the grave so the guard could substitute it.
stories.summary: A mourning widow at her husband's grave was seduced by a man guarding the body of someone the king had executed. When that body was stolen, she had her husband disinterred so the guard could put it in its place. The incident shows temptation persists even in mourning.

stories.actor: A belt seller and a man
stories.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman selling belts and asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it back.
stories.turn: She took it and remained silent.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled she could claim she was merely taking back her own property, so she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man grabbed one. When she demanded it back, he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he returned it; she took it silently. Rav Nahman ruled she could say she was only taking what was hers.

stories.event: Rav Aha spent the night in a study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.turn: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon died, and the next day he rebuked the townspeople for endangering him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha slept in the study hall where a demon lurked. It appeared to him as a seven-headed serpent, and each time he bowed in prayer one head fell off. The next morning he told the townspeople that without a miracle they would have endangered him.

stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna, so Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head covering and learned it was because he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When he came, Rav Huna noticed he did not cover his head, and Rav Hamnuna explained he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come before him until he married.

stories.event: Rav Rehumi, who came home every Yom Kippur eve, stayed engrossed in study one year.
stories.turn: His waiting wife was distressed and shed a tear.
stories.outcome: The roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and always came home on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he became absorbed in study and did not come; his wife kept expecting him and finally shed a tear. At that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: Yehuda came home every Friday at twilight, preceded by a pillar of fire seen by his father-in-law Rabbi Yannai.
stories.turn: One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared he must be dead.
stories.outcome: The words acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya studied all week and returned home every Shabbat eve, with a pillar of fire going before him. One week he stayed late at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the fire, said to overturn his bed since he must have died. His statement came true and Yehuda died.

stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died when the marriage contract was about to be written.
stories.outcome: Investigating, they found a genealogical mismatch: Rabbi descended from David's wife, Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with a daughter of Rabbi Hiyya's household, but the girl died just as the ketuba was to be written. Rabbi wondered if there was some flaw in the families. Examining the lineage, they found Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride, the son reduced it to six years, then decided to marry first.
stories.outcome: Ashamed before his father, he was reassured that he acted as God did, citing verses; the story continues past the window.
stories.summary: Rabbi then arranged a match with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, who agreed to support the groom for twelve years of study. When the bride was shown to him he asked for six years, and when shown again said he would marry first and then study. He was ashamed before his father, who told him he had his Maker's insight, as God too advanced His plan to dwell among Israel.

stories.event: Rav Rehumi, who came home every Yom Kippur eve, stayed engrossed in study one year.
stories.turn: His waiting wife was distressed and shed a tear.
stories.outcome: The roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava and always returned home on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he stayed absorbed in study; his wife waited and finally shed a tear. The roof beneath him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: Yehuda came home every Friday at twilight, preceded by a pillar of fire seen by Rabbi Yannai.
stories.turn: One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead.
stories.outcome: The statement came true and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya came home each Shabbat eve with a pillar of fire before him. One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the fire, ordered his bed overturned as for a mourner. Like an error from a ruler, it came true and Yehuda died.

stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died as the marriage contract was being written.
stories.outcome: They found a genealogical mismatch between the families.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry a girl of Rabbi Hiyya's household, but she died as the ketuba was about to be written. Suspecting a flaw, they examined the lineage. Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital, while Rabbi Hiyya descended from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.event: Rabbi's son was matched with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter on condition of twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: Seeing her, he chose to marry first; after twelve years away she became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi weighed divorce or a second wife, and instead the husband prayed for her and she was healed.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son was to study twelve years before marrying a daughter of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, but on seeing her he reduced it to six and then married her first; his father reassured him he had acted like God. He then studied twelve years away, and returned to find his wife infertile. Rabbi rejected both divorce and a second wife as unjust to her, so the husband prayed and she was cured.

stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall at the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, refusing to wait for him.
stories.turn: He stayed twelve years.
stories.outcome: When he returned, the town's paths had changed and he could not find his way home; the story continues past the window.
stories.summary: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding celebration, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai set off for the study hall. Rabbi Shimon asked him to wait so they could go together, but he did not. He studied for twelve years, and by the time he came back the streets had changed and he did not know the way to his house.

stories.event: Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast, vowing to fall and drown if anyone cited a baraita he could not derive from a mishna.
stories.turn: An old man challenged him with a baraita about a dying man's instructions to give his sons a shekel weekly.
stories.outcome: Ilfa identified it as following Rabbi Meir's view in the mishna and met the challenge.
stories.summary: Passed over for head of the academy, Ilfa suspended himself from a ship's mast and declared he would drop into the sea if anyone brought a teaching of the school of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya that he could not trace to a mishna. An old man cited a baraita on a father's deathbed allowance for his sons. Ilfa answered that it follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one must fulfill the instructions of the dead, and so he succeeded.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya Arikha and his mother-in-law
stories.event: Rav Hiyya supported his brother's widow for twenty-five years in her father's house, then refused her further sustenance and her ketuba.
stories.turn: Rabba bar Sheila ruled for her and wrote an authorization to seize his property, which Rava upheld.
stories.outcome: When she then claimed the produce, Rava found the authorization defectively written and denied her the produce.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya Arikha supported his widowed sister-in-law, who was also his mother-in-law, for twenty-five years, but then refused her both sustenance and her ketuba. She sued before Rabba bar Sheila, who ruled she had not claimed only out of embarrassment and ordered payment; when Rav Hiyya ignored him he authorized her to seize his property, and Rava said the ruling was good. But when she asked Rava for the produce since then, he examined the document, found it lacked the statement that the property was the deceased's, and ruled it defective, rejecting all her counter-arguments.

stories.event: Walking outside Eretz Yisrael, they saw men sowing mixed seeds, and one proposed excommunicating them.
stories.turn: The other said he misunderstood the law.
stories.outcome: Both times the other refused, explaining these plantings were not forbidden there.
stories.summary: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling and saw a man sowing mixed seeds; one suggested they ostracize him, but the other said he did not understand these laws. They then saw a man sowing wheat and barley among vines, and again one wanted to ostracize him. The other explained that by Rabbi Yoshiya's view this is not liable unless sown together in one hand motion.

stories.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself permitted it for men of fit morals.
stories.outcome: Rav replied that he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not themselves.
stories.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were on the road behind a woman, and Rav urged Rav Yehuda to walk quickly away from her. Rav Yehuda reminded him that he had ruled such seclusion permitted for upright men. Rav answered that he did not mean people like them, but men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

stories.event: Rav Amram was climbing a ladder toward a woman when he stopped himself halfway.
stories.turn: He cried out 'Fire in Amram's house', bringing the Sages, and accepted their shame over shame in the World to Come.
stories.outcome: He adjured his evil inclination to leave him; it emerged as a pillar of fire, and he declared himself its master.
stories.summary: Halfway up the ladder, Rav Amram braced himself and shouted that there was a fire in his house. The Sages came and said he had embarrassed them, but he said better to be ashamed now than in the World to Come. He made his evil inclination leave him; it came out like a pillar of fire, and he told it that though it was fire and he only flesh, he was stronger.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river.
stories.turn: He began crossing on a rope bridge toward her.
stories.outcome: Halfway across, Satan left him, saying only Heaven's warning to protect him had spared him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the other side of a river, and with no ferry he started across a rope bridge. Halfway over, Satan let him go and said that were it not for Heaven's proclamation to protect Rabbi Meir, his life would have been worthless.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree.
stories.outcome: Halfway up, Satan left him, saying only Heaven's warning had spared him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he began to climb. Halfway up Satan released him, saying that only Heaven's proclamation protecting him had saved him.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily cursed Satan, received Satan disguised as a repulsive pauper on Yom Kippur eve.
stories.turn: The pauper pretended to die after being rebuked, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man.
stories.outcome: Peleimu hid in the outhouse; Satan revealed himself and told him to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan'.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say every day, 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a pauper, demanded to be brought inside and seated at the table, then behaved disgustingly and spat into a cup; when rebuked he collapsed as if dead, and people shouted that Peleimu had killed a man. Peleimu fled and hid, and when Satan saw his distress he revealed himself and told him to say, 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.'

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: His wife, puzzled by his prayer against the evil inclination though he had long withdrawn from her, disguised herself as the prostitute Haruta.
stories.turn: He propositioned her and they had relations; at home he confessed, and she revealed it was she.
stories.outcome: He said he had intended to sin, and fasted the rest of his life until he died of it.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination, which puzzled his wife since he had abstained from her for years. She adorned herself and passed him in his garden as Haruta the prostitute; he propositioned her and fetched her a pomegranate as payment. At home he sat in the lit oven in remorse; she proved it had been her, but he said he had still meant to sin, and fasted until he died.

stories.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Two Sages stood for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not.
stories.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rava poured drinks for the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rose before him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda did not. Rava was angered and asked whether only they were Sages and the others not.

stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa poured drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the latter did not rise before him. Rav Pappa was offended.

stories.event: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood serving drinks at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and objected when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests and Rabbi Tzadok cited God's providing for all, justifying it.
stories.summary: At Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding, the Nasi himself stood and poured for Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Eliezer would not take the cup and rebuked Rabbi Yehoshua for accepting it. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served guests he took for Arabs, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself sets a table for every creature.

stories.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money for oxen.
stories.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
stories.summary: A man sold Rav Pappa a field to raise money to buy oxen. In the end he did not need it. Rav Pappa gave him back his land, acting beyond what the law required.

stories.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
stories.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
stories.turn: Wheat arrived, and it emerged the ship had already been near when they sold.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the mansions return to their owners, defending the ruling to Rami bar Shmuel.
stories.summary: In a famine in Neharde'a people sold their mansions to buy wheat, but then wheat arrived. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their owners, since the ship was already in the river bends at the time of sale. Rami bar Shmuel objected that this would discourage buyers, and Rav Nahman replied droughts are not daily, to which Rami said in Neharde'a they are frequent.

stories.event: A man gave Rav Anan a gift as a scholar; Rav Anan accepted it and referred his case to Rav Nahman, saying he was disqualified.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative and favored him, so his opponent was intimidated and lost.
stories.outcome: Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan, then returned after his fast but frightened him, so he learned sitting in a box, producing the two Orders of Elijah.
stories.summary: The man told Rav Anan he wanted him to accept the gift as one brings first fruits; Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified. Rav Nahman took the man for Rav Anan's relative, put aside an orphans' case to hear his, and the honor shown silenced the opposing litigant. Elijah, who had been teaching Rav Anan, left him; after fasting Elijah returned but frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box to learn, hence Seder Eliyahu Rabba and Zuta.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandchild to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
stories.turn: Asked why, he cited the verse linking teaching grandchildren to standing at Sinai.
stories.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying a child to the synagogue, hastily wrapped in a simple head covering. He asked what the rush was, and Rabbi Yehoshua answered that teaching one's grandchildren is likened to receiving the Torah at Horeb. After that Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never ate breakfast before reviewing with his child and adding to his lesson.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
stories.event: A widow claiming her ketuba from the orphans was told by them to dress properly for court.
stories.turn: She put on all her clothes.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled with Rav that a widow's clothes on her are appraised toward her ketuba.
stories.summary: A widow of the bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court for her ketuba. They said it shamed them for her to go in house clothes, so she dressed in all her garments. Ravina ruled, following Rav, that whatever she is wearing is appraised and deducted from her ketuba.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives and their stepmother
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened by their stepmother's spending, were advised by him to have their father set aside land for her sustenance.
stories.turn: After the father died, Reish Lakish ruled the land only added to her support and threatened them when they cited Rabbi Yohanan.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing since an equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives complained that their father's wife was squandering his money on her upkeep, and he advised them to have their father allot her a field for sustenance. After their father died, Reish Lakish ruled that this only increased what she could draw and threatened them harshly when they cited Rabbi Yohanan. They complained to Rabbi Yohanan, who said he could do nothing, since a colleague of equal standing disagreed.

stories.event: At his death the Angel of Death was sent to do his bidding, and he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the angel's knife.
stories.turn: Shown his place, he jumped into paradise and swore not to leave.
stories.outcome: God let him stay since he never annulled an oath; he returned the knife at a Divine Voice's command, and met Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai there.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to grant his wishes; he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the knife so he would not be frightened. When lifted to see it, he leapt over into paradise and swore he would not come back; God ruled that since he had never had an oath annulled he could stay, and a Divine Voice made him return the knife. Elijah announced him, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned him about whether a rainbow had appeared in his lifetime.

stories.event: When dying, Rabbi Hanina asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his learning, then for the knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting the same trick as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
stories.outcome: At his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone, and it withdrew only when Rabbi Alexandri appealed to his own honor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, a friend of the Angel of Death, asked for thirty days to review his studies, then asked to see his place and to hold the knife. The angel refused, asking if he meant to repeat Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's trick, and dismissed his claim of having kept the whole Torah since he had not tended the afflicted. When he died a pillar of fire surrounded him, and it lifted only when Rabbi Alexandri asked him to remove it for his own honor.
